mood_contract: Deepened unease: the student leaves unsettled about whether they can trust what the agent says and does, and holding a repeatable loop instead of certainty. Unease is the designed mood, not a failure.

intended_learnings.text: Certainty is not on offer; the loop is assess, mitigate, reassess the residual, decide. "I can't tell" is a real answer, and the residual risk is something you write down.

Well-formed English is the attack surface: an agent treats text it reads (a source, a web page, a file) as possible instructions, directly or indirectly. No employee reads every document as an instruction; an agent does.
Same prompt, same files, different session, different answer: one run is a sample, so a check has to be repeatable.
Scope beats patch: the best mitigation is the access you never grant. Ask what is the worst thing it could do with that access.
Agent mitigations (scope, split, filter, gate, review) sit on top of normal company security controls, never in place of them.
A judgement you will repeat gets packaged as a reusable check (a skill) that you run again, rather than re-prompted from memory each time.
When judgement runs out, escalate to a person; a prototype that works for you is not yet fit for production.

answer_tokens.m4-what-matters.txt: Before authoring the security skill, the participant dictates 3-5 lines of what this check must catch in THEIR system (their own voice, not generic GDPR).
answer_tokens.m4-grill-answers.txt: The agent grills the participant about the security skill (which lens matters, which data they fear leaking, injection worry, tool reach, which policy rules matter, report shape). The participant answers the whole grill in one message and tells the agent to save.
answer_tokens.m4-chosen-risk.txt: After the audit, the participant picks ONE risk to mitigate, names the mitigation shape (scope, split, filter, gate or review), and asks the agent to re-run the check and state the residual.
